strengths: The problem of obtaining theoretical guarantees on adversarial risk and the dependence on the structure of the data is well-motivated of interest to the community.
The direction of studying the interplay between feature learning and adversarial robustness appears to be novel.
The paper is well written and describes the setup, literature well.
The proofs are easy to follow.

The paper’s first contribution is that the ground truth latent features are in fact the optimal features in terms of adversarial robustness. This is not largely surprising, but it plays an important role in informing the kinds of algorithms one should use to achieve an adversarially robust model. They then show how to characterize the sample complexity and model complexity for just adversarially training the second layer for a broad class of target functions when given access to a feature learning oracle. Importantly, these bounds are independent of the ambient dimension as the hardness only depends on the effective dimension of the problem. These results are an interesting extension of previous works in feature learning for 2-layer neural networks which do not consider adversarial robustness.

Although I do not have any particular knowledge in robust training, I found the paper accessible and well explained. The stakes are clearly presented in the introduction. Additionally, the setup and the assumptions are generally well motivated.

Despite not having read the proofs in detail, I appreciated that the proof techniques originate from diverse ideas and prior works including statistical learning, with generalization bounds provided in Appendix C1, geometrical analysis from the low-dimensional subspace assumption, approximation of functions using infinite-width neural networks, etc.
From the references provided in the introduction, it is clear that this paper offers new results and insights, distinguishing this work from previous research in the field.
The numerical experiment displayed in the main text gives a nice support to the theoretical claims of the paper.
The question of robust learning in the multi-index model is well-motivated by the authors. Authors clearly state the assumptions and limitations of their results.

As the main result, authors prove that in the multi-index model, sample complexity of adversarial training is the same as in standard training. They combine prior work on feature learning with a second stage adversarial training which requires careful technical analysis. Authors also provide experiments to support their claim.

The contribution is good because it is a new theoretical study for adversarial feature learning for learning multi index models, which has been gaining traction recently. Their main results highlight that robust learning is achievable without a significant increase (at least for some functions) in sample complexity. Moreover, the oracles assumed for learning the target subspace can be realized by training the first layer in a 2 layered neural network. Overall, this is a well structured, theoretically sound work with a good upshot and I recommend an accept.
This paper * presents results with clarity and precision, offering complete proofs, insightful comments, and remarks that make the content accessible and well-structured
leverages previous results and introduces interesting, non-trivial findings in a rigorous framework (e.g. the possibility of performing standard feature learning to obtain optimal adversarial risk)
validates its theoretical results with numerical simulations
acknowledges its limitations and open problems.

Interesting problem: Understanding the effects of adversarial training of neural networks on the sample complexity may be significant for the deep learning literature. Furthermore, this paper combines two lines of work: 1) feature learning in two-layer neural networks and 2) adversarially robust learning in linear and random feature models.
Theoretical study under reasonable assumptions: The authors study the problem under reasonable assumptions (in line with the prior work such as Hassani & Javanmard, 2024).

Provides a valuable insight into the problem: The paper shows that the adversarial training does not significantly (in the order of dimensions) affect the sample complexity in comparison to standard training.

Good enough presentation: The paper answers most of the questions a reader may have, which is the main criterion when assessing the quality of the presentation. However, I think it is not an easy-to-follow paper. Instead, some parts of the paper require back-and-forth reading, which may be acceptable for such a theoretical paper.
weaknesses: The extent of the theoretical novelty in the analysis and unexpectedness of the result is unclear in the paper's presentation.
The paper would improve by emphasizing the central difficulties in combining the finite-dimensional guarantees with feature learning results.
It would be useful to know what parts of the analysis would change if one were directly studying the setup of random features on finite dimensions.

The role of the low-dimensionality of the target subspace and feature learning is primarily in obtaining a second layer with dimension-independent norm ($r_a$ in Algorithm 1) that fits the target allowing for the Rademacher-complexity argument to go through, which is the same as generalization bounds in existing works on feature learning such as Damian et al. 2022.
The DFL definition lacks an explicit statement that the weights $w_i$ are assumed to be on the unit sphere; the definition should be self-contained and not rely on implicit assumptions.

The connection between the DFL assumption and the specific optimization algorithms used to train the first layer is not clearly explained, leaving a gap in understanding how this assumption is practically achieved.

The major weakness is the lack of extensive experiments; the first row of Figure 1 is not a fair comparison because it graphs a model trained completely using adversarial training techniques versus just training the last layer using adversarial techniques while initializing the first layer to the ground truth representation.
It would be interesting to see how different combinations of standard vs. adversarial training on different network layers for real-world data affect performance.

The statement of Theorem 1 is confusing: it is not clear that the multi-index data model is still assumed, and the phrase “with equality when f^* in F” is confusing since f* in F doesn’t imply equality; also the statement “Further, h is represented as E[]” is confusing because it seems to mean that any h that satisfies the theorem must be represented in that way, which is not true.
Theorems 4, 5, 6 and 7 rely on specific activations (ReLU / polynomial); it is unclear how the proofs would extend to more general activations like sigmoid or tanh, limiting practical applicability.
The proof of Theorem 1 could be replaced with an outline of the proof ideas; the full proof interrupts the flow of the paper and could be better placed in the appendix.
A paragraph or two summarizing the main steps or ideas of the proofs of the main theorems would help the reader; currently the reader must piece together the proof techniques from the appendix.

The claim that the bounds derived do not depend on the dimension, which includes the optimal adversarial risk (defined in equation 2.2), lacks an explicit statement in the main text explaining why the optimal adversarial risk is dimension-independent.

Several concepts and notations are not clearly defined, such as the Landau notations in the main results; it is unclear whether the obtained bounds are non-asymptotic or asymptotic and with respect to which variable, and whether hidden constants depend on the dimension or other parameters.
The result is limited to $\ell_2$ norm perturbations; the paper lacks discussion on extension to $\ell_\infty$ norm and why current proof techniques cannot tackle this setting.

Theorem 1 relies on the squared loss assumption; for classification tasks logistic loss would be more natural, and the implications of this limitation on applicability to practical scenarios should be discussed.
Organization of the main text is hard to follow; the theorems for SFL and DFL are more or less copies of each other, stated in different places, and could be combined for clearer presentation.
Proof of Lemma 16 in the Appendix is hard to follow due to typos and undefined symbols ( $\tilde k_i$ defined with $k_i$ and $k'_i$ before they are defined).
For pseudo-Lipschitz functions, while the sample complexity is independent of $d$, there is an exponential dependence on $k$, which seems quite high.

Many mathematical terms could benefit from more intuition for first-time readers; for example, clarification in Theorem 1 of the random variables with respect to which the expectation is taken in the towering property.

It is unclear what $\beta$ represents in the SFL oracle and whether a lower bound on $d\mu/d \tau_k$ connects to Assumption 1; also Assumption 1 may not hold for natural scenarios where $x$ has a low rank structure and $\tilde Ux$ may not vary independently from $Ux$.
The results rely on the assumption of independence between the coordinates $x_\parallel$ and $x_\perp$ (Assumption 1), which may be a limitation.
The work does not characterize robust test risk, focusing only on sample complexities, unlike prior works that provide asymptotic characterizations of robust test risk.

There is a significant gap to practice: assumptions such as subGaussian input, implicit assumptions on inputs and labels, the first layer being trained with adversarial loss in practice, limitation to $\ell_2$ perturbations, constant adversary budget $\epsilon = O(1)$ versus practical $\epsilon = O(\sqrt{d})$, and only polynomial and ReLU activations considered.
Numerical results and their discussion are limited; most of Section 5 describes the experimental setting with little insight into the results, and several details (e.g., Figure 1) are missing.
